summary: Denmark lies in Northern Europe, made up of the Jutland peninsula and several hundred islands; it is a monarchy with a long history, known for its high-welfare society, LEGO and the fairy tales of Andersen.

ranking.name: Lutheranism (Church of Denmark)
ranking.description: Around 965, King Harald Bluetooth proclaimed on the Jelling Stone that he had “made the Danes Christian.” In 1536 Christian III carried out the Reformation, confiscated the property of the Catholic Church and made Lutheranism the state religion. The 1849 constitution designated it the “People’s Church,” supported by the state; citizens become members when baptized at birth and pay the church tax, so the registration rate is high, but in practice very few people attend church.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: Denmark is a highly secularized Nordic welfare state in which education, healthcare and social assistance have long been provided by the state rather than the church. Many people remain in the state church but rarely engage with religion in their lives; others formally leave to avoid paying the church tax, and those who have left the church together with non-believers among the descendants of immigrants make up the non-religious population.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: From the late 1960s Denmark recruited foreign workers from Turkey, Pakistan, Yugoslavia and elsewhere, and in the 1980s and 1990s it took in refugees from Lebanon, Iran, Iraq, Somalia and Bosnia, making Muslims the largest minority religious group. In 2005 the publication of the Muhammad cartoons by Jyllands-Posten provoked an international controversy, and religion and immigration remain pivotal issues in Danish politics today.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: After the Reformation of 1536 Catholicism was banned in Denmark, and it became legal again only when the 1849 constitution guaranteed religious freedom. Today’s Catholics are mostly immigrants from Poland, the Philippines, Vietnam and elsewhere, and their descendants.

religion.background: Denmark was Christianized by King Harald Bluetooth at the end of the Viking Age in the 10th century, and in the Middle Ages the Catholic Church held vast lands and power. The Reformation of 1536 established Lutheranism as the state religion, and from then on state and church were closely intertwined. The democratic constitution of 1849 guaranteed religious freedom and established the People’s Church, and the folk high school movement promoted by the 19th-century theologian Grundtvig also profoundly influenced Danish religion and education. In the late 20th century Denmark became highly secularized, while immigrants brought new religions such as Islam.

language.official: Danish is the official language; the Faroe Islands and Greenland have their own separate official languages.

ranking.name: Danish
ranking.description: Danish belongs to the North Germanic branch and developed from the Old Norse of the Viking Age. During the Hanseatic League period in the Middle Ages it absorbed a great deal of Low German vocabulary, and the Bible of Christian III, published in 1550, laid the foundation of the written language. From 1380 to 1814 Denmark and Norway shared a monarch, and Danish was also Norway’s written language; today Danish is the nation’s official and educational language, and is also used in some settings in the Faroe Islands and Greenland.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: Denmark recruited Turkish guest workers in the late 1960s, and after the 1970s, through family reunification, the Turkish community settled in cities such as Copenhagen and Aarhus, becoming one of the largest immigrant language groups; most of the second generation and later use both Danish and Turkish.

ranking.name: German
ranking.description: Southern Jutland (northern Schleswig) once belonged to German states, passed to Prussia after the Second Schleswig War of 1864, and after a plebiscite in 1920 the northern part returned to Denmark, leaving a German-speaking minority. In 1955 Denmark and Germany issued the Bonn–Copenhagen Declarations guaranteeing the rights of the minorities on both sides, and the area still has German schools and newspapers.

language.history: Danish derives from Old Norse, with inscriptions written in runes in the Viking Age, and gradually diverged from Swedish and Norwegian from about the 12th century. In the Middle Ages it was strongly influenced by Low German, and the Danish Bible and printed works after the Reformation established the written language. During the Denmark–Norway union Danish was the administrative language of both countries, and after Norway separated in 1814 the two developed separately. In the 19th century national romanticism promoted Danish literature and education, and in the late 20th century immigrants brought languages such as Turkish and Arabic.

ranking.name: Smørrebrød (open-faced sandwich)
ranking.description: Buttered rye bread is covered with toppings such as pickled herring, liver pâté, roast beef, small shrimp or egg, piled in layers and eaten with knife and fork.
ranking.history: The name means “butter and bread,” and it was originally rye bread with leftovers that farmers and workers ate for lunch in the fields. In the late 19th century restaurants in Copenhagen began to refine it, and Oscar Davidsen’s restaurant, opened in 1888, became famous for a very long menu of hundreds of combinations. It is the core of Danish lunch culture, and the “Christmas lunch” (julefrokost) before Christmas is incomplete without all kinds of open sandwiches and schnapps.

ranking.name: Stegt flæsk (crispy fried pork belly)
ranking.description: Thick slices of pork belly are fried until golden and crisp and served with boiled potatoes and plenty of parsley sauce, with a salty, rich flavor; it is a typical Danish home dinner.
ranking.history: From the late 19th century Denmark developed a strong pig-raising and pork-export industry through the farmers’ cooperative movement, and the first cooperative slaughterhouse was founded in Horsens in 1887, after which pork became the most common meat of the Danes. In a national dish vote held by the Danish Ministry of Food in 2014, this humble home-style dish stood out and was officially chosen as the national dish, reflecting the food traditions of Denmark’s agricultural society.

ranking.name: Frikadeller (Danish meatballs)
ranking.description: Ground pork, or mixed ground pork and veal, is mixed with onion, egg and breadcrumbs and shaped into flat oval meatballs, which are pan-fried in butter until golden.
ranking.history: The name is generally thought to have been borrowed through German, and similar meatballs are found across Northern Europe and Germany. The Danish version is the most typical home dinner, often served with potatoes, brown gravy and pickled red cabbage, and when cold can be sliced and put on an open sandwich. It appears on family tables, in school lunch boxes and at gatherings, and for many Danes it is the “taste of mother’s cooking” and one of the dishes from home that Danes abroad miss most.

ranking.name: Æbleskiver (ball-shaped pancakes)
ranking.description: Batter is cooked in a special cast-iron pan with hemispherical hollows into small round pancakes, slightly crisp outside and soft inside, eaten with jam and powdered sugar.
ranking.history: The name means “apple slices,” because in the early version a slice of apple was wrapped into the batter, though most are now made without it. It is a representative treat of Advent and the Christmas season in Denmark, traditionally enjoyed with hot spiced mulled wine (gløgg), and is often prepared at Christmas gatherings in schools, workplaces and homes. The special pan is a utensil that many Danish families pass down through generations.

ranking.name: Wienerbrød (Danish pastry)
ranking.description: A laminated pastry dessert made by repeatedly rolling and folding many layers of butter and dough, filled with almond paste, custard or jam, and glazed with icing after baking.
ranking.history: The Danes call it “Viennese bread,” because during a bakers’ strike in Copenhagen in 1850, the shops instead hired bakers from Austria and elsewhere, who brought the Viennese technique of laminated dough. After the strike ended, Danish bakers learned and improved the method, adding more butter and filling to form a distinctive style. In the late 19th century this pastry spread around the world with immigrants and bakers, which is why it is called “Danish pastry” in English.
